blocks.text: Edwin Hubble established the foundation for modern cosmology by demonstrating that galaxies are moving away from the Earth, and their velocity increases with distance. In other words, the farther a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away. This observation led to Hubble's law, which states that:

blocks.title: Hubble's law
blocks.text: The recession velocity v of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance d from the Earth.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Before Hubble's discovery, most scientists thought the universe was static. Hubble's law turned that idea on its head, suggesting the universe had a beginning, leading to the Big Bang theory.
Here v is the recession velocity and d is the distance. Hₒ is called Hubble's constant and its value is 2.3×10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.

Fig. 21.6 illustrates graphical representation of Hubble's law, revealing a direct and linear relationship between the redshift of galaxies and their distance from Earth. As the distance increases, the recession velocity also increases, providing a strong evidence for an expanding universe. The slope of this linear trend corresponds to the Hubble constant (H₀), which quantifies the rate of cosmic expansion.

blocks.alt: Graph with Recession velocity on the vertical axis and Distance on the horizontal axis. Many dots lie close to a straight line through the origin, with a dense cluster in the middle.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.6: Graphical representation of Hubble's law (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.6).

blocks.title: Brain Teaser
blocks.text: A galaxy is moving away from us very fast. According to Hubble's Law, what does that tell us about its distance?

All the galaxies in the universe are moving away from each other. An observer in another galaxy will observe the same effect. This is happening because space itself is stretching. An inflated-balloon model is often considered by scientists to explain the Big Bang expansion, as shown in Fig. 21.7. The dots which are marked on the surface of a balloon represent the galaxies, and the skin of balloon represents four dimensional space-time. As the balloon is inflated, every dot “sees” the other dots moving away. This is similar to how galaxies move apart in space. This model helps us to understand two main ideas. First, no matter where we are in the universe, we would see galaxies moving away from us. This means the expansion is happening everywhere, and there is no special centre. Earth is not at the centre of the universe. The universe is expanding now, we can conceptually reverse time. Doing so implies:

items: in the past, galaxies were closer together.
going further back, all matter was compressed into a very small, dense, and hot state.

blocks.alt: Three dark balloons of increasing size, each with grid lines and the same light dots at the same places; on the larger balloons the dots are farther apart.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.7: Analogy of the expanding universe: dots move apart as the balloon inflates (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.7).

blocks.text: This idea forms the basis of the Big Bang Theory, which proposes that the universe began from an initial singularity about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since. Hubble's law provides strong observational evidence that the universe is not static but expanding, which is one of the key pillars supporting the Big Bang model.
An approximate timeline for the evolution and expansion of the universe from the Big Bang till present is presented in Fig. 21.8.

blocks.alt: A cone widening upwards from the Big Bang at the bottom. Stages up the cone with times: Big Bang, 0; Recombination Era, 380 thousand years; First stars appear, 300 million years; Early galaxies, 1 billion years; Modern galaxies (Acceleration), Today. Small labels: First structure formation; Expanding proto-clusters; Current Era: Lambda-CDM, with arrows showing galaxies moving apart.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.8: Approximate timeline of the universe's evolution from the Big Bang to present (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.8).

blocks.text: Satellite remote sensing is a powerful technology that uses sensors aboard orbiting spacecraft to monitor and analyze Earth's environment from space. It enables scientists to track phenomena such as deforestation, climate change, ocean temperatures, and atmospheric composition. Unlike ground-based methods, it offers wide geographic coverage and repeated observations over time, making long-term environmental monitoring possible.

blocks.alt: The Sun (Energy source) shines on the Earth (Target). Rays from the Earth go up to a satellite (Sensor), passing a point where radiation is scattered in all directions. The satellite sends signals down to a dish and buildings (Processing station); a thick arrow carries the data to a person at a computer (Analysis), and then to a laptop showing a coloured map (Application).
blocks.caption: Figure 21.9: The remote sensing process (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.9).

blocks.text: Following are the steps of satellite remote sensing:

items: Source and Illumination: The first and foremost element of SRS is source or illumination, which illuminates the target. It is in form of electromagnetic radiation.
Atmosphere: After radiations are emitted from source, they interact with atmosphere. This interaction may be in the form of scattering, reflection etc.
Interaction with Target: After atmospheric interaction comes interaction with target of interest that this interaction depends on the properties of the target and radiation.
Recording with Sensor: The emitted or reflected radiations from target are recorded by sensors which are remote (not in contact with target).
Transmission and Reception: The recorded radiations from sensor are then transmitted to the reception station to convert the data into understandable form of images, etc.
Interpretation and Analysis: The processed image is then interpreted (to get information) electronically or digitally.
